lessons.title: One-sided inequalities on a number line
lessons.summary: Read and draw a ray using its boundary, direction and open or filled circle.
lessons.objective: Read and draw a ray using its boundary, direction and open or filled circle.
lessons.before: Numbers become greater as you move to the right. A negative number further left is smaller.
lessons.ideas:
‘Less than’ and ‘greater than’ exclude the boundary. ‘At most’ and ‘at least’ include it. For example, ‘at most 4’ is \(x\leq 4\).

Use an open circle for \(\lt,\ \gt\) and a filled circle for \(\leq,\ \geq\). Mark a ray towards smaller numbers for less than, and towards greater numbers for more than.

The statements \(-2\lt x\) and \(x\gt -2\) describe the same values. If the original sign includes equality, keep equality when swapping sides.
lessons.method:
What do the words tell me about the boundary?

Identify the value that separates the allowed values from the others. Then decide whether that value itself is allowed.

Which way does the ray go?

The line shows a range of real numbers. A ray marks all points on one side of a boundary, including values between the labelled integers.

What if the variable is written second?

Read the comparison in the order written. If you put the two sides in the opposite order, change the direction of the sign.
mistakes: ‘At least 4’ includes 4 and values greater than 4. It does not start just after 4.
The arrow shows the direction of the allowed numbers. An open circle describes the endpoint only.
The negative sign of a boundary does not reverse the ray. Compare the actual values on the line.

examples.title: Turn words into a one-sided inequality
examples.question: Write an inequality for the statement ‘\(x\) is less than \(4\)’.
examples.solution:
Use \(4\) as the boundary.

The wording excludes the boundary.

The inequality is \(x\lt 4\).

  2. Filled circle and an arrow to the right.

examples.solution:

examples.title: Read a statement with the variable on the right
examples.question: Rewrite \(-4\gt x\) with \(x\) first.
examples.solution:
The sign in \(-4\gt x\) compares \(-4\) with \(x\).

When the order of the two sides is swapped, the sign is read the other way. Include equality exactly as before: \(x\lt -4\).

lessons.title: Bounded intervals and integer solutions
lessons.summary: Read two endpoint types, write one chained range and identify the integers it contains.
lessons.objective: Read two endpoint types, write one chained range and identify the integers it contains.
lessons.before: Use an open circle to exclude an endpoint and a filled one to include it.
lessons.ideas:
The left boundary goes first in a chained inequality. For example, \(-1\leq x\lt 4\) means x is at least −1 and less than 4.

The conditions \(x\gt -3\) and \(x\leq 2\) are both true on \(-3\lt x\leq 2\). Draw only that segment and its correct circles.

For \(-2\leq x\lt 3\), the integers are \(-2,\,-1,\,0,\,1,\,2\). Zero is an integer, and the open right endpoint excludes 3.
lessons.method:
How do I read two boundaries together?

A segment shows values between two endpoints. Each circle tells you separately whether its own endpoint is included.

What does ‘and’ mean for a range?

A value must satisfy both conditions joined by ‘and’. It lies in the common part of the two rays.

How do I list only the allowed integers?

A range normally includes real numbers. When an answer asks for integers, select only the whole-number points that satisfy the range.
mistakes: A filled circle on one end says nothing about the other end. Read the two signs separately.
Marking both entire rays would include values that satisfy just one of the limits.
For a non-integer bound, avoid rounding it and accidentally including the wrong integer. Move to the first actual integer inside the interval.

examples.title: Read a bounded solution from a number line
examples.question: Give the single inequality in x shown on the number line.
examples.solution:
Read left to right between \(-2\) and \(1\). The segment requires both conditions.

The left boundary is included. The right boundary is excluded. Write \(-2\leq x\lt 1\).

examples.title: Combine two inequalities using and
examples.question: Write one inequality to show that \(x\geq -4\) and \(x\lt -1\).
examples.solution:
Start at the left boundary \(-4\). Rewrite the lower condition with this number first.

Follow the number line to the right boundary \(-1\). Keep both endpoint conditions: \(-4\leq x\lt -1\).

examples.title: Check each candidate against both bounds
examples.question: From \(-4,\quad -3,\quad -1,\quad 1,\quad 2\), give every value that satisfies \(-3\leq x\lt 1\).
examples.solution:
The first and last candidates lie outside the interval. \(-1\) lies strictly inside it.

Test the endpoints against their own signs. The allowed candidates are \(\left\{-3, -1\right\}\).

lessons.title: Solve linear inequalities (Extended)
lessons.summary: Isolate a variable and reverse the inequality exactly when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
lessons.objective: Isolate a variable and reverse the inequality exactly when multiplying or dividing by a negative.
lessons.before: Be able to expand a single bracket and solve a linear equation in one variable.
lessons.ideas:
For \(5x+2\lt 17\), subtract 2 and divide by 5. You get \(x\lt 3\). Keep the strict sign through both operations.

From \(9\gt 4\) comes \(-9\lt -4\). Follow the same rule when dividing by a negative number. Keep the presence or absence of equality.

Move the smaller x-coefficient first to obtain a positive variable term when possible. Clear positive denominators before collecting terms if that simplifies the working.
lessons.method:
Which operations preserve the direction?

Add or subtract the same amount on both sides to keep the comparison true for the same values. A positive scale factor also preserves order.

Why does a negative multiplier reverse the sign?

On the number line, multiplying by −1 reflects the values about zero. The order changes even when the original two numbers were both positive.

How do I solve with variables on both sides?

If x appears twice, bring the variable terms together and the numbers together. Keep each whole side of the inequality consistent.
mistakes: The result is a range of x-values. A single value at the boundary is not a complete answer.
Adding or subtracting a negative amount does not reverse a sign. Reversal is for multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
If you exchange the complete left and right sides to write x first, reverse the written comparison so it still states the same order.

examples.title: Solve an inequality with a positive coefficient
examples.question: Solve \(2x+3\leq 6\). Give the whole solution.
examples.solution:
Subtract \(3\) from both sides to get \(2x\leq 3\).

Divide by positive \(2\). The inequality sign keeps the same direction.

Write the final range as \(x\leq \frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Reverse the sign when dividing by a negative
examples.question: Solve \(-2x+4\lt 1\). Give the whole solution.
examples.solution:
Subtract \(4\) to get \(-2x\lt -3\).

Divide by \(-2\). Reverse the inequality sign because the divisor is negative.

Write the final range as \(x\gt \frac{3}{2}\).

examples.title: Clear a positive denominator
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{3x-2}{2}\geq 2\). Give the whole solution.
examples.solution:
Multiply by \(2\) to get \(3x-2\geq 4\). Keep the sign because the denominator is positive.

Add \(2\) and then divide by \(3\).

Write the final range as \(x\geq 2\).

lessons.title: Chained inequalities and whole-number decisions (Extended)
lessons.summary: Solve both parts of a chained inequality and interpret the bounds in contexts such as budgets.
lessons.objective: Solve both parts of a chained inequality and interpret the bounds in contexts such as budgets.
lessons.before: Know the lower and upper endpoint rules and why dividing by a negative value reverses an inequality.
lessons.ideas:
From \(1\leq 2x+3\lt 9\), subtract 3 throughout and divide by 2. The result is \(-1\leq x\lt 3\).

When rewriting the result from the lower endpoint to the upper endpoint, use the inclusivity signs that belong to those same endpoint values.

For a maximum budget, find the largest allowed integer. For a minimum total, choose the smallest allowed integer. The sign tells you what to do if a boundary is itself a whole number.
lessons.method:
What should I do to all three parts?

A chain compares its middle expression to two different bounds. Applying the same inverse operation to all three expressions is a compact way to solve both comparisons.

What happens if the middle coefficient is negative?

A negative divisor reverses the left comparison and the right comparison. The resulting chain can be written with the greater number first.

How do I turn a range into a usable result?

The answer to a real-valued inequality can be a range. The requested number of objects may be restricted to whole numbers.
mistakes: Subtracting a number only from the middle expression changes the conditions.
One inequality may be strict while the other is inclusive. Check that each endpoint still has its own type after changing direction.
Ordinary rounding can violate the requirement. A bound of \(x\geq 4.1\) requires at least five whole units.

examples.title: Solve a chained inequality by acting on all three parts
examples.question: Solve \(1\leq 2x+3\leq 11\).
examples.solution:
Subtract \(3\) from all three expressions.

Divide all three by \(2\). The coefficient is positive, so both signs stay the same. The answer is \(-1\leq x\leq 4\).

examples.title: Clear a denominator in a chained inequality
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{1}{2}\leq \frac{x+3}{2}\lt \frac{5}{2}\).
examples.solution:
Multiply all three parts by \(2\). This is positive, so the signs remain unchanged.

Subtract \(3\) from all three parts to obtain \(-2\leq x\lt 2\).

examples.title: Form a budget inequality and find a whole number
examples.question: A print order costs £6 to set up and £4 per poster. The budget is at most £18. Find the greatest number of posters that can be ordered.
examples.solution:
Let \(x\) count posters. The budget gives \(4x+6\leq 18\), with \(x\) a non-negative integer.

Subtract the set-up price and divide by the price per poster: \(x\leq 3\).

The largest allowed integer is \(3\). The next integer exceeds the budget.

lessons.title: Plot a linear inequality in two variables (Extended)
lessons.summary: Draw the boundary, choose its line style and shade the unwanted half-plane.
lessons.objective: Draw the boundary, choose its line style and shade the unwanted half-plane.
lessons.before: Know how to plot a vertical or horizontal line and find two points on a straight line.
lessons.ideas:
Use a solid line for \(\leq\) or \(\geq\). Those signs admit equality. Use a broken line for \(\lt\) or \(\gt\) because the boundary itself is excluded.

Cambridge uses shading for the unwanted half-plane unless the question directs otherwise. Shade the other side if your test point satisfies the inequality.

Check the equation, then use the wanted side to choose whether the comparison is smaller or greater. Include equality on a solid line only.
lessons.method:
What separates the wanted and unwanted sides?

Replace the inequality sign with equality to find a straight boundary line. Plot two suitable points unless the line is horizontal or vertical and you can locate it directly.

How do I decide which side fails the inequality?

An off-line point tells you whether its whole half-plane is wanted. If substitution gives a true statement, that side is wanted.

How do I read a horizontal, vertical or sloping boundary?

For a vertical line compare x-coordinates. For a horizontal line compare y-coordinates. For a sloping line, rearranging the inequality for y may make above or below clear.
mistakes: The style of the line does not tell you which side to shade. Make the side decision separately.
If the origin lies on the boundary, it cannot distinguish the two sides. Test a different easy point.
The visual edge of the printed grid is not a boundary of the inequality unless the question draws or states it as one.

examples.title: Choose how to draw the boundary
examples.question:
Which line style is used for the boundary of \(x+y\lt 2\)?

  1. Broken
  2. Solid
examples.solution:
Replace the sign with equality to get \(x+y=2\).

Use a broken boundary because equality is excluded.

examples.title: Read a horizontal boundary
examples.question:
Which condition describes the unshaded part of this graph?

  1. \(y\leq 1\)
  2. \(y\geq 1\)
  3. \(y\lt 1\)
  4. \(x\leq 1\)
examples.solution:
The horizontal boundary has equation \(y=1\).

The wanted area is below the boundary. The line style gives the inequality \(y\leq 1\).

examples.title: Use an off-line point to choose the side
examples.question:
For \(x+y\lt 0\), use \(\left(1,1\right)\) as a test point. Where does it lie?

  1. The test point is on the wanted side
  2. The test point is on the unwanted side
examples.solution:
The origin is on this boundary, so choose another point.

At \(\left(1,1\right)\), the left side has value \(2\). The comparison \(2\lt 0\) is false.

The test point is on the unwanted side.

lessons.title: Draw and describe a region (Extended)
lessons.summary: Use the overlap of satisfying half-planes and list every inequality that defines a region.
lessons.objective: Use the overlap of satisfying half-planes and list every inequality that defines a region.
lessons.before: Draw a straight boundary, choose its line style and test an off-line point.
lessons.ideas:
Under the usual Cambridge convention, the clear part satisfies every condition. Label it R. You can test a point inside R in all the original inequalities.

For each line, choose a point strictly inside R to determine the sign. Then use the line style to decide about equality. List all the conditions together.

A point on any broken line fails the strict inequality for that line. A corner only counts if all adjacent boundaries allow equality and every other condition is true.
lessons.method:
How do I draw the overlap of several conditions?

Draw the boundary for every inequality. Choose solid or broken separately for each. Then remove each unwanted half-plane by shading it.

Which inequalities define the region shown?

Read the shape's boundary lines from their intercepts or points. If needed, use two visible points to find the gradient of a sloping line.

How do I check points on a boundary or corner?

Test a boundary point against every condition. An included point may lie on a solid boundary if it satisfies the rest of the system.
mistakes: Even if a point passes two conditions, it belongs outside R if it fails a third. Find the overlap, not a single satisfying half-plane.
The shaded side is normally unwanted. If a question explicitly shades R itself, interpret the shaded part as wanted for that question.
An unshaded segment drawn with breaks is an excluded boundary. The line style still matters after shading.

examples.title: List all inequalities that define the region
examples.question:
The area marked R is left clear. Choose the list of inequalities defining R.

  1. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)
  2. \(x\leq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)
  3. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\gt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)
  4. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\geq 4\)
examples.solution:
Compare x to the vertical line \(x=1\). The line type and position of R give \(x\geq 1\).

Compare y to the horizontal line \(y=1\). The line type and position of R give \(y\lt 1\).

Compare an interior point with the sloping line \(x+y=4\). The line type and position of R give \(x+y\leq 4\).

All of these restrictions must hold together: \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\).

examples.title: List all inequalities that define the region
examples.question:
In this question the wanted region R is shaded. Choose the list of inequalities defining R.

  1. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\gt 2\)
  2. \(x\leq 1\), \(y\gt 2\)
  3. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 2\)
  4. \(x\geq 1\), \(y\geq 2\)
examples.solution:
Compare x to the vertical line \(x=1\). The line type and position of R give \(x\geq 1\).

Compare y to the horizontal line \(y=2\). The line type and position of R give \(y\gt 2\).

All of these restrictions must hold together: \(x\geq 1\), \(y\gt 2\).

examples.title: Test every inequality before accepting a point
examples.question:
Which point satisfies all the conditions \(x\gt 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\)?

  1. \(\left(2,0\right)\)
  2. \(\left(0,0\right)\)
  3. \(\left(1,1\right)\)
  4. \(\left(2,2\right)\)
examples.solution:
Check x and y first. The first boundary accepts the selected point with \(x=2\). The y-coordinate is \(0\), which is strictly below \(1\).

The sum of its coordinates is \(2\) and satisfies \(x+y\leq 4\). Thus \(\left(2,0\right)\) meets all the conditions.

1. From \(\left(1,0\right)\), \(\left(0,0\right)\), \(\left(1,1\right)\), \(\left(2,2\right)\), state which point satisfies all the conditions \(x\geq 1\), \(y\lt 1\), \(x+y\leq 4\). Show your tests.

    [2]

  2. From \(\left(3,1\right)\), \(\left(1,1\right)\), \(\left(2,2\right)\), \(\left(3,3\right)\), state which point satisfies all the conditions \(x\gt 2\), \(y\lt 2\), \(x+y\leq 5\). Show your tests.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Check x and y first. The first boundary accepts the selected point with \(x=1\). The y-coordinate is \(0\), which is strictly below \(1\).

The sum of its coordinates is \(1\) and satisfies \(x+y\leq 4\). Thus \(\left(1,0\right)\) meets all the conditions.

(b)

Check x and y first. The first boundary accepts the selected point with \(x=3\). The y-coordinate is \(1\), which is strictly below \(2\).

The sum of its coordinates is \(4\) and satisfies \(x+y\leq 5\). Thus \(\left(3,1\right)\) meets all the conditions.
